source.title: Improving Data Efficiency via Curating LLM-Driven Rating Systems
source.authors: Jinlong Pang; Jiaheng Wei; Ankit Parag Shah; Zhaowei Zhu; Yaxuan Wang; Chen Qian; Yang Liu; Yujia Bao; Wei Wei

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study's own instruction-tuning results argue that smaller, curated datasets can outperform full datasets, qualifying quantity-based expectations for downstream performance. It does not test pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The relevant reported outcomes are downstream benchmark averages for 10K DS2-selected samples compared with the 300K full-data baseline, with the rating model varied. Other method comparisons and the data-budget curves in Figure 5 are not separately extracted as scaling-law results: the text gives no curve values or fitted scaling relationship.
record.test_reason: This is a data-selection method paper for instruction tuning. Its 'challenge to data scaling laws' rests on its own method (DS2, 10K) beating full-data fine-tuning (300K). It reports no pretraining loss, no model-size or compute sweep, no fitted power law, and no downstream-vs-scale or downstream-vs-pretraining-loss relation. So it does not test V1–V7. Its scaling-law language is framing, and the comparisons are method-vs-baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, with one qualification: the authors' claim concerns instruction-tuning data quantity, not pretraining scaling laws. They conclude that a curated 3.3% subset beats the full 300K pool and matches or beats LIMA, so quality matters more than quantity in instruction tuning and 'data scaling laws' should be rethought. Their evidence is their own method against baselines, not a scaling fit.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates data curation and instruction fine-tuning outcomes, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss across model sizes, token counts, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports results across different rating models and data budgets; it also notes that the diversity score is not uniformly effective across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: With random selection, 30x more instruction-tuning data barely changes downstream averages. LLaMA-3.1-8B: random 10K 57.4 vs full 300K 57.7. Mistral-7B: 49.3 vs 50.6. LLaMA-2-7B: 35.8 vs 38.0. Figure 5 curves reportedly show that curated subsets beat larger budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream benchmark gains from increasing supervised fine-tuning data quantity are small and can be outweighed by data selection quality.

record.problems: The relevant comparison changes both data quantity and data selection/quality, so it does not isolate a dataset-size effect. The paper reports no fitted power-law curves or uncertainty estimates for these comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows left out. Figure 5's data-budget curves are not extracted because the text gives no curve values or fitted scaling relation.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; not studied.
Extrapolation of power-law fits; not studied.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count; not studied.
Power-law form in fine-tuning or other regimes. Figure 5 shows benchmark scores versus fine-tuning sample count, but with no loss, no fit and no readable values.
Downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss. Only fine-tuning data selection and quantity vary; base models are 7B/8B only.
Dependence of exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices; not studied.

missing.what: Random-selection 10K versus full 300K comparisons, the only quantity contrast with selection held random (57.4 vs 57.7; 49.3 vs 50.6; 35.8 vs 38.0). Relevant only to a fine-tuning data-quantity claim, not to V1–V7.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link and limits_scope label are not supported. V6 concerns predictability with model scale or pretraining loss, and these rows are method-vs-baseline comparisons that confound quantity with selection. I reclassified the study as discusses/T6 with no verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power-law fits from small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Whether power-law loss curves hold in fine-tuning or other training regimes; the study reports downstream task scores, not a fitted power law in loss.
Model-scale and pretraining-loss predictability; the reported results concern downstream task scores after instruction fine-tuning with curated versus full data.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LLaMA-3.1-8B fine-tuned on DS2-selected data, across the three reported rating models
reader_labels.reason: The study reports higher benchmark averages for a curated 10K subset than for the 300K full-data baseline, showing that downstream performance need not track dataset quantity alone in this fine-tuning setting (r1–r3).
